questions.question: What does X25519 take as inputs and produce as output?
options: A 32-byte scalar and a 32-byte u-coordinate, producing a 32-byte u-coordinate
Two affine points (x, y) producing a third affine point (x, y)
A field prime p and curve parameter A producing a generator point
A hash digest and a nonce producing a signature
questions.explanation: X25519 is defined as a scalar multiplication function on the u-coordinate with 32-byte inputs/outputs.

questions.question: What is the purpose of X25519 scalar clamping?
options: Force the private scalar into a safe shape (e.g., fixed top bits and a multiple of the cofactor)
Make the output u-coordinate unique by rejecting non-canonical inputs
Allow computing y-coordinates from x-coordinates without square roots
Speed up inversion by replacing it with table lookups
questions.explanation: Clamping masks specific bits so the scalar has required properties used by the design and security analysis.

questions.question: In the Montgomery ladder used by X25519, what does the pair of registers (X2:Z2) and (X3:Z3) typically represent during the loop?
options: Two consecutive multiples of the input point, enabling differential addition
The x- and y-coordinates of the same point in affine form
Two random points unrelated to the input to hide leakage
A hash state and a message block being compressed
questions.explanation: The ladder maintains a “consecutive multiples” invariant so each bit step can do one add and one double using x-only formulas.

questions.question: Why does X25519 not need the y-coordinate during scalar multiplication?
options: Montgomery curves admit x-only differential addition and doubling formulas in projective (X:Z) form
The y-coordinate is always zero on Curve25519
The y-coordinate cancels out because the curve has cofactor 1
The protocol replaces y with a hash of x
questions.explanation: The Montgomery ladder can update x-coordinates using only x(P), x(Q), and x(P−Q), avoiding y.

questions.question: How is an X25519 u-coordinate encoded on the wire?
options: 32 bytes little-endian representing an integer modulo p (with the top bit masked on decode)
32 bytes big-endian representing an integer modulo p (reject non-canonical values)
A pair of 32-byte big-endian integers (x, y)
A compressed Edwards encoding with a sign bit
questions.explanation: RFC 7748 defines little-endian byte strings and requires masking the most significant bit when decoding X25519 inputs.

questions.question: Attack scenario: why do many protocols recommend rejecting an all-zero X25519 shared secret?
options: Because small-order inputs can force the output to all-zero, yielding a predictable shared secret if accepted
Because all-zero indicates the field prime p was chosen incorrectly
Because all-zero implies the private scalar was not clamped
Because all-zero proves the peer’s public key is on a different curve
questions.explanation: An attacker can sometimes supply a low-order public input; the all-zero check makes that case fail closed.

questions.question: What does a constant-time `cswap` aim to prevent in a ladder implementation?
options: Branching or memory-access patterns that reveal scalar bits through side channels
Mathematical invalidity due to using the wrong curve parameter A
Collision attacks on the encoding of u-coordinates
Forgeries in signature schemes like Ed25519
questions.explanation: If swaps depend on secret bits, a branchy swap can leak the scalar through timing/power/cache behavior.

questions.question: Why is a pure-Python X25519 implementation still not production-safe, even if it follows the RFC formulas?
options: The Python runtime and big integers are not constant-time, so secret-dependent timing/caching can leak information
Because RFC 7748 forbids implementing X25519 outside of C
Because Python cannot handle 255-bit integers correctly
Because Curve25519 requires floating-point arithmetic to be correct
questions.explanation: Constant-time behavior depends on the entire stack; Python big-int operations and interpreter behavior vary with values.
